Randomisation lists for a trial

Source: R/rndalc.R
rndalc.Rd

Allocates participants to arms by simple, permuted-block or stratified block randomisation from a seed, so that the list can be made again exactly from the seed and the settings, in R or on the command line.

Usage

rndalc(
  n = NULL,
  arms = c("A", "B"),
  ratio = rep(1, length(arms)),
  block = c(2, 3) * sum(ratio),
  strata = NULL,
  seed = NULL,
  prefix = "P"
)

# S3 method for class 'rndalc'
print(x, ...)

Arguments

n

The number of participants: a whole number from 1 to 10000000. With strata it may be left out (it is their total).

arms

The names of the arms: two or more, each once.

ratio

The allocation ratio: one whole number from 1 per arm.

block

The block sizes drawn from: whole numbers, each a multiple of sum(ratio); 0 for simple randomisation.

strata

NULL, or the strata and their places: a named vector of whole numbers from 0.

seed

NULL (drawn from R's generator, so set.seed() fixes it) or a whole number from 0 to 2147483647.

prefix

The start of the participant ids: one string.

x

An object of class rndalc.

...

Not used by print().

Value

An object of class rndalc, a list: alloc, a data frame in enrolment order with id, stratum (with strata), block (the block's number within its stratum; NA for simple randomisation) and arm; tab, the participants of each arm by stratum (a matrix, one row all without strata); and seed, the seed used.

Details

With block = 0 each participant is allocated alone (simple randomisation), to arm a with chance ratio[a] / sum(ratio). Otherwise blocks are made one after another, each of a size drawn with equal chances from block (every size a multiple of sum(ratio)), holding the arms in the ratio in an order drawn uniformly (a Fisher-Yates shuffle). Block sizes drawn at random keep the next allocation hard to guess at a site (Schulz and Grimes 2002). The list stops at the places asked for, so the last block of a stratum may be incomplete. With strata, each stratum has its own sequence of blocks (Rosenberger and Lachin 2016, ch. 3).

The draws come from the package's own generator (xorshift64* seeded through splitmix64; Vigna 2016), the same on every platform; the seed is returned with the list. Sealing the list (a commitment signed and timestamped before enrolment) is left to other tools.

References

Rosenberger, W. F. and Lachin, J. M. (2016). Randomization in Clinical Trials: Theory and Practice, 2nd ed. Wiley. doi:10.1002/9781118742112

Schulz, K. F. and Grimes, D. A. (2002). Generation of allocation sequences in randomised trials: chance, not choice. The Lancet, 359(9305), 515-519. doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(02)07683-3

Vigna, S. (2016). An experimental exploration of Marsaglia's xorshift generators, scrambled. ACM Transactions on Mathematical Software, 42(4), 30. doi:10.1145/2845077

Examples

a <- rndalc(40, seed = 12)
a
#> rndalc: 40 participants, seed 12
#>      A  B
#> all 20 20
head(a$alloc)
#>    id block arm
#> 1 P01     1   A
#> 2 P02     1   B
#> 3 P03     1   A
#> 4 P04     1   A
#> 5 P05     1   B
#> 6 P06     1   B
s <- rndalc(arms = c("drug", "placebo"), ratio = c(2, 1),
            strata = c(Toronto = 30, Ottawa = 24), seed = 7)
s$tab
#>         drug placebo
#> Toronto   21       9
#> Ottawa    16       8
rndalc(20, block = 0, seed = 1)$tab
#>      A B
#> all 13 7
